title: A4 — Cost-optimized compute
bodyMarkdown:
## Cost-optimized compute

Exam task **4.2**. This lesson is the compute side of cost optimization: choosing the right billing model, right placement model, and right scale pattern before your workload starts burning money. In production, compute cost mistakes usually come from confusion between options that look similar at first glance. The exam is designed around those confusions, so each section below teaches direct contrasts you can reuse in scenario questions.

### K01 ? AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

Cost management features answer two practical questions: **who spent the money** and **who should receive discounts**. For ownership, cost allocation tags are the first control. AWS billing reports do not use your user-defined tags until you activate the tag key in Billing and Cost Management. Teams often miss this and assume tagging alone is enough. It is not. You apply tags on resources, then separately activate those keys so billing pipelines include them.

For organization-wide optimization, consolidated billing in AWS Organizations treats member accounts as one billing family for commitment discounts. Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discount sharing is on by default, so one account can buy a commitment and another account can consume the matching usage benefit. This is a major cost lever for multi-account environments because fragmented usage often leaves discounts unused unless sharing is enabled.

For finance workflows, treat governance and visibility as different controls. Tags and account structure provide attribution. Commitment sharing improves effective unit price. Budgets and anomaly tools provide guardrails, but they do not replace tagging hygiene.

**Exam tip:** if a stem says "tags are applied but not visible in billing," the missing step is activating cost allocation tags.

### K02 ? AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

Use each tool for its intended decision. **Cost Explorer** is for analysis and forecasting: visualize spend trends, filter by account, service, or tags, and model likely future spend. **AWS Budgets** is for policy thresholds: alert when actual or forecasted cost crosses a limit and trigger actions. **Cost and Usage Report** gives comprehensive line-item data for deep chargeback, custom BI, and SQL-based audit workflows.

The confusion to avoid is "reporting" versus "control." Cost Explorer explains what happened. Budgets can notify and automate responses. CUR feeds custom data models when prebuilt dashboards are too coarse. In exam scenarios, if leadership wants near-real-time warning before overrun, Budgets is the control plane. If they want forensic detail across all usage dimensions, CUR is the raw dataset.

Also remember refresh cadence and intent. Budget thresholds are planning controls, not emergency kill switches by default. They must be configured with notifications or actions. Cost Explorer is excellent for trend questions but not a direct enforcement mechanism.

**Exam tip:** "visualize and forecast" points to Cost Explorer, "alert or action on threshold" points to Budgets, and "most granular billing dataset" points to CUR.

### K03 ? AWS global infrastructure (for example, Availability Zones, AWS Regions)

Compute cost and availability decisions depend on where workloads run. An AWS Region is a separate geographic area; Availability Zones are isolated locations inside that Region. AWS also defines Local Zones and Wavelength Zones for latency-sensitive edge patterns. You should map workload class to location class before choosing instance strategy.

For production systems, a core reliability and cost rule is to deploy across at least two AZs. Single-AZ placement looks cheaper until a zonal disruption turns into outage cost. Multi-AZ design usually increases baseline resource count, but it lowers business interruption risk and reduces emergency re-architecture pressure.

Placement has network-price implications too. For example, NAT gateway pricing includes hourly plus per-GB processing charges, and AWS specifically recommends aligning resources with NAT gateways in the same AZ to reduce transfer charges. So infrastructure topology directly changes compute-adjacent cost.

Use Regions for sovereignty, major latency domains, and disaster boundaries. Use AZs for fault isolation. Use Local Zones or Wavelength only when end-user latency or edge processing justifies them.

**Exam tip:** if the scenario is "production app, stay online during an AZ issue," default to multi-AZ design first, then optimize cost inside that shape.

### K04 ? AWS purchasing options (for example, Spot Instances, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans)

This is one of the highest-value contrast areas on SAA-C03. **On-Demand** is maximum flexibility with no commitment. EC2 usage is billed in one-second increments with a 60-second minimum for supported operating systems, so you pay for runtime without long-term lock-in.

**Spot Instances** use spare EC2 capacity and can be much cheaper, but they can be interrupted when AWS needs capacity back. You receive a two-minute interruption notice, which means Spot is best for fault-tolerant, checkpointed, or queue-based work.

**Reserved Instances** and **Savings Plans** both trade commitment for lower price. Reserved Instances commit to specific EC2 dimensions for 1-year or 3-year terms with All Upfront, Partial Upfront, or No Upfront payment options. Savings Plans commit to spend measured in dollars per hour for 1 or 3 years. Compute Savings Plans are broader and can apply across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda, while EC2 Instance Savings Plans are narrower but can provide deeper discount in exchange for instance-family-plus-region commitment.

The common confusion is capacity versus price. Savings Plans discount price but do not provide capacity reservations by themselves. If a workload needs guaranteed zonal capacity, evaluate capacity reservation design separately from discount instruments.

**Exam tip:** Spot for interruptible jobs, Reserved or Savings for predictable baseline, On-Demand for burst and unknowns.

### K05 ? Distributed compute strategies (for example, edge processing)

Distributed compute is about putting processing near users, data sources, or dependent systems while controlling spend. In AWS, that often means deciding among Regional deployment, Local Zones, Wavelength Zones, or on-premises extension.

Local Zones are built for low-latency workloads near population centers without running your own local datacenter. Wavelength is for ultra-low-latency 5G-connected use cases by placing compute and storage in telecom provider environments. Outposts keeps workloads on-premises while using AWS services and APIs.

Cost-optimized distributed design avoids overusing edge locations for workloads that do not need them. Edge footprint increases operational complexity and can require extra replication, observability, and traffic management. Keep control planes and durable system-of-record components regional unless latency requirements force distribution.

A practical exam pattern is to separate **interactive latency path** from **backend processing path**. Put the minimum required component at the edge, then push everything else into Region where service breadth and cost controls are stronger.

**Exam tip:** choose edge placement only when the requirement explicitly states strict latency or local processing needs.

### K06 ? Hybrid compute options (for example, AWS Outposts)

Hybrid compute questions test whether you can match constraints like data residency, local system dependency, and latency-to-facility requirements. Outposts is explicitly designed to extend AWS infrastructure and services into on-premises facilities with consistent APIs and operating models.

Contrast this with Local Zones and Wavelength. Local Zones are AWS-managed locations near end users, not your server room. Wavelength is mobile edge in telecom networks for 5G endpoints. Outposts is your environment, AWS hardware and control model.

Cost optimization in hybrid designs comes from minimizing duplicate platforms. If teams run separate tooling stacks for cloud and on-prem, operational cost rises fast. Outposts can lower that integration overhead when constraints force local deployment anyway. But do not choose Outposts just because "hybrid" sounds future-proof. If the workload can run in Region or Local Zone without hard on-prem dependency, those are usually simpler.

Keep service status awareness sharp: AWS Snow Family is closed to new customers, so do not treat legacy Snow devices as a current default option for new hybrid compute planning.

**Exam tip:** if the workload must remain on-premises yet use native AWS APIs, Outposts is the direct fit.

### K07 ? Instance types, families, and sizes (for example, memory optimized, compute optimized, virtualization)

EC2 type names encode selection logic. Instance naming has family and size components. In `c7g.xlarge`, `c` indicates compute-optimized series, `7` is generation, `g` indicates Graviton option, and `xlarge` is the size.

Family choice should follow bottleneck type, not habit. Compute-heavy services generally map to C families, memory-bound services to R or X families, balanced app tiers to M families, bursty low baseline tasks to T families, and accelerator-dependent workloads to appropriate G, P, Trn, or Inf families.

Generation and option letters matter for price-performance. Newer generations often improve performance per dollar. Option letters identify CPU vendor or capabilities that affect licensing, throughput, and runtime behavior.

Right family selection is one of the easiest compute cost wins because it removes chronic overprovisioning. Teams often buy larger sizes in the wrong family to compensate for a mismatched resource profile.

**Exam tip:** pick family by dominant resource bottleneck first, then tune size.

### K08 ? Optimization of compute utilization (for example, containers, serverless computing, microservices)

Utilization optimization asks: how much idle capacity are you paying for? EC2 gives maximum control but requires you to manage host capacity and patching. Fargate removes host management for containers and bills per second for requested vCPU and memory, with a 1-minute minimum for Linux and 5-minute minimum for Windows containers. Lambda prices functions by request count plus execution duration and is strongest for event-driven burst patterns.

The cost confusion is assuming serverless is always cheaper. Serverless eliminates idle-host waste, but long-running steady tasks can be cheaper on right-sized EC2 commitments. Microservice decomposition can improve utilization by scaling only busy components, but too much fragmentation can add orchestration overhead.

Also compare runtime constraints. Lambda has a maximum timeout of 900 seconds for standard functions, so jobs requiring long uninterrupted execution may fit Fargate or EC2 better unless they can be split.

For exam scenarios, tie service choice to execution model: short event handlers and spiky APIs align with Lambda, containerized services with predictable runtime and no host management align with Fargate, specialized or continuously running workloads align with EC2.

**Exam tip:** optimize utilization by matching billing unit to workload behavior: function invocation, container task runtime, or VM uptime.

### K09 ? Scaling strategies (for example, auto scaling, hibernation)

Cost-optimized scaling keeps enough capacity for SLOs without paying for sustained idle headroom. Target tracking scaling policies automate this by adding capacity when metrics exceed target and removing capacity when metrics fall below target.

Horizontal scaling adds instances or tasks; vertical scaling increases size of an instance. Horizontal typically improves fault tolerance and incremental growth control. Vertical can be fast for monolithic bottlenecks but may introduce restart events and bigger failure domains.

For EC2 lifecycle controls, understand stop versus hibernate. Stopping clears RAM and preserves EBS volumes. Hibernation saves RAM to the EBS root volume, allowing faster resume for pre-warmed states. In both cases, you do not pay instance usage while stopped, but you still pay for EBS storage. Hibernation helps workloads with long startup phases where resume time has monetary value.

Do not confuse hibernation with elasticity. Hibernation preserves state of an instance; Auto Scaling changes fleet capacity. They solve different cost problems.

**Exam tip:** auto scaling handles dynamic demand; hibernation is a startup-time optimization for specific EC2 instances.

### S01 ? Determining an appropriate load balancing strategy (for example, Application Load Balancer compared with Network Load Balancer compared with Gateway Load Balancer)

Select by traffic layer and feature need. ALB is Layer 7 for HTTP and HTTPS and supports application-aware routing such as host-based and path-based behavior. NLB is Layer 4 for high-performance transport traffic and supports static IP patterns that many partner allowlists require. GWLB operates at network layer behavior for virtual appliance insertion, such as centralized firewall or deep packet inspection flows.

Cost-effective choice means avoiding over-featured load balancing. If you only need TCP pass-through and static addresses, NLB is usually cleaner than ALB-plus-workarounds. If you need URL routing and app-aware logic, ALB prevents costly custom proxy tiers. If you need inline appliance scaling and a single traffic entry-exit model, GWLB avoids bespoke packet steering systems.

Exam distractors often swap ALB and NLB. Use protocol and routing requirement to separate them quickly.

**Exam tip:** choose ALB for HTTP routing intelligence, NLB for transport-level performance and static IP, GWLB for appliance traffic chaining.

### S02 ? Determining appropriate scaling methods and strategies for elastic workloads (for example, horizontal compared with vertical, EC2 hibernation)

Start with elasticity shape. Use horizontal scaling when load varies and workload can run multiple parallel units behind a load balancer or queue. This aligns with target tracking policies and typically gives smoother cost control under demand swings.

Use vertical scaling when software is hard to distribute or bottlenecks are tightly coupled to single-node resources. Vertical resizing can be valid for stateful or legacy components, but it reduces granularity and can raise blast radius.

Use hibernation only for special cases where restoring in-memory state is valuable, such as expensive cache warm-up. It does not replace scale-out policy. Hibernation can reduce warm-up delay cost, while scaling policies reduce mismatch between demand and provisioned capacity.

In exam designs, look for words like "unpredictable traffic," "independent request units," and "maintain availability during spikes" to favor horizontal. Look for "single process with large memory footprint" for vertical candidates, then evaluate downtime tolerance.

**Exam tip:** horizontal scaling is usually the default for elastic web and API tiers; hibernation is a niche optimization, not a scaling strategy.

### S03 ? Determining cost-effective AWS compute services with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Lambda, Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate)

Use Lambda for event-driven, short-running logic where per-request and duration pricing tracks bursty demand efficiently. Use Fargate when you want container packaging without EC2 host management. Use EC2 when you need full OS control, unusual runtime dependencies, specialized hardware, or continuously running workloads where commitments can lower cost.

The best choice depends on workload profile, not service popularity. Lambda can become expensive for extremely high sustained duration workloads compared with steady reserved compute. Fargate avoids host operations but bills for requested container resources continuously while tasks run. EC2 can be cheapest for stable baseline when paired with Savings Plans or Reserved commitments, but only if you actively right-size and autoscale.

When the scenario includes strict execution time beyond Lambda limits, move toward Fargate or EC2 unless the job can be decomposed into chained steps.

**Exam tip:** map first by execution model, then by cost instrument: Lambda for event bursts, Fargate for managed containers, EC2 for deep control and long-running steady compute.

### S04 ? Determining the required availability for different classes of workloads (for example, production workloads, non-production workloads)

Workload class drives availability spend. Production customer-facing systems should run across at least two AZs and include health-based traffic shifting. This raises baseline cost but protects revenue and trust.

Non-production classes can accept lower redundancy when business impact is lower. Development or ephemeral test systems often use smaller footprints and shorter runtime windows. The cost goal is to avoid applying production-level redundancy everywhere by default.

A useful decision pattern is to assign explicit recovery and uptime targets by class. If outage cost is high, pay for multi-AZ and faster failover. If outage cost is low, use leaner topology, strict schedules, and automatic teardown.

Do not blindly copy production architecture into all environments. A cost-optimized portfolio intentionally mixes resilience levels by business criticality while keeping security controls intact.

**Exam tip:** production tier usually implies multi-AZ resilience; non-production can trade availability for lower spend when requirements allow.

### S05 ? Selecting the appropriate instance family for a workload

Family selection should follow measured utilization. If CPU is consistently high while memory is moderate, compute-optimized families are likely better than simply scaling a general-purpose family upward. If memory pressure dominates with modest CPU, memory-optimized families reduce waste.

Bursty low-average workloads can benefit from burstable families, while accelerator-driven ML or graphics workloads need matching accelerator families rather than oversized general-purpose nodes. Storage-heavy patterns may need storage-optimized families.

This is a cost discipline problem: right family first, then right size. Wrong family causes persistent overpayment because you buy excess of one resource to satisfy shortage of another.

On the exam, family mistakes hide behind "works fine" distractors. Several options can function, but only one aligns with the resource profile at lowest recurring cost.

**Exam tip:** choose family by bottleneck signature from metrics, not by existing team habit.

### S06 ? Selecting the appropriate instance size for a workload

After family selection, size tuning controls incremental cost. Instance sizes in a family usually scale resources stepwise. For example, in C7g, `large` is 2 vCPU and 4 GiB, `xlarge` is 4 vCPU and 8 GiB, and `2xlarge` is 8 vCPU and 16 GiB. This doubling pattern helps estimate price-performance transitions.

Sizing strategy: start from measured peak plus safety margin, then scale iteratively. Oversizing every node "just in case" is one of the most common EC2 waste patterns. Combine right-size reviews with Auto Scaling so you do not lock high spend into off-peak periods.

Also include billing granularity in decision timing. EC2 On-Demand per-second billing with a 60-second minimum supports fine-grained experimentation and rapid resize validation. You can test smaller candidates safely, observe headroom, and roll forward.

In exam scenarios, eliminate extremes. Tiny sizes that cannot satisfy baseline are wrong, but oversized choices that ignore utilization evidence are also wrong.

**Exam tip:** right-size with metrics and family-consistent steps; moving one size down across many instances is often a major savings lever.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
